insight.title: The Missing Decimal That Cost a Mars Mission
insight.subtitle: A simple unit conversion error caused a $125 million orbiter to disintegrate in the Martian atmosphere.
insight.notificationHook: A math error destroyed a Mars probe

sections.text: In 1999, the Mars Climate Orbiter approached the red planet to begin its mission. NASA engineers waited in the control room, expecting a routine orbital insertion as the craft dipped behind the horizon.

Deep in the flight software, a tiny human error hid in plain sight. One team used metric Newtons for thrust calculations, while another used imperial pound-seconds. The discrepancy was never caught during peer reviews.

As the orbiter attempted its burn, the navigation system miscalculated the trajectory. It descended too low into the Martian atmosphere, lost structural integrity under the friction, and vaporized in the thin, alien air.
The universe does not forgive a rounding error.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. This is the clear, plain version of today's news.

Ukraine struck Russia's Crimean bridge for the second night in a row. Russia struck two major bridges in Kyiv called the Northern and Southern bridges. Russia's defence ministry said it downed 1,441 Ukrainian drones in a major overnight barrage. The strikes come ahead of a meeting in China between presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin. Trump said the fighting in Ukraine would be among the topics discussed in the talks.

Nvidia warned chip buyers that proposed US legislation could expose them to US legal action. The Remote Access Security Act would give the US Commerce Department tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centers to access Nvidia chips. Nvidia messaged chip buyers to caution that the law would give the government broader authority over cloud services. The company said for now it would not sell chips to customers who rent over 50 percent of their graphics processing units to Chinese companies.

Turning to politics, 32 percent of Americans approve of President Donald Trump's performance in the White House, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll. The four-day poll surveyed 1,521 US adults nationwide and had a margin of error of about three percentage points. Trump's popularity has fallen as the US war with Iran has pushed fuel prices higher. Just 31 percent of Americans support the war in Iran.

The United States has lost its measles elimination status after recording over 5,400 cases this year. The Pan American Health Organization confirmed the decision following a rise in cases that is more than double last year's total. A country loses elimination status when population immunity lowers enough for sustained spread of the disease. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention tallied 5,412 cases to date in 2026, resulting in more than 590 hospitalizations and at least six deaths.

The US dollar held at April 2025 highs as markets awaited comments from US Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh. The dollar index advanced for a fifth straight day, up 0.1 percent at 103.52, its highest in 19 months. The greenback was buoyed after hawkish comments from several Fed officials and hotter-than-expected US inflation data raised bets for rate hikes. Meanwhile, Japan's economy contracted by an annualised 0.1 percent in the July-to-September quarter.

European Union countries accused Russia of trying to drag out talks on ending the war in Ukraine while it bombs power plants. The bloc imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions. EU foreign ministers said the priority in Ukraine should be to secure a ceasefire and then a real peace agreement. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told reporters that Russia started the war and must make concessions.

Next, how the energy transition only works if development works.

The energy transition must support socioeconomic development to succeed across Asia and the Pacific, according to a recent survey. The Economic and Social Survey of Asia and the Pacific 2026 notes that fossil fuel prices influence inflation, trade balances and public budgets. Indonesia lowered gasoline subsidies from 3.2 percent to 1.0 percent of GDP in 2014, and redirected the savings into infrastructure and social protection. India’s solar manufacturing incentive scheme catalyzed 48 gigawatts of manufacturing capacity and is projected to save about US$1.8 billion annually in foreign exchange. Nepal expanded electricity coverage from 53 percent to 95 percent of the total population between 2010 and 2024.

Next, researchers have mapped the basal ganglia, which are structures in the human brain that are key to learning and controlling motor skills. The basal ganglia occupy about 2 percent of the brain volume, roughly the size of a gumball. Researchers looked at more than 25 million cells from humans, macaques and marmosets. The work is published by Cell Press as the culmination of three years of scientific work funded by the National Institutes of Health. Researchers expect to have a dataset for the whole brain by the end of next year.

Turning to energy, livestock manure is driving Denmark’s biogas boom. Denmark produces more than 17 million tonnes of manure annually, according to the Danish Agriculture and Food Council. The country has upscaled a handful of small biogas operations into about 150 industrial-sized plants. Today, Denmark has Europe’s highest share of biogas in its gas grid, at about 40 percent. In Sonderborg, ProjectZero aimed to create a carbon-neutral energy system by the end of 2029, cutting energy-related carbon emissions by 79 percent so far.

In shipping news, Shanghai has reached its highest-ever global ranking for maritime port operations. Shanghai has risen to second place in a ranking of major global maritime hubs. The Chinese megacity secured the spot largely on the strength of its combined industrial and tech capabilities.

In the United States, the electric grid operator PJM Interconnection proposed a plan to federal energy regulators to speed up power plant and data centre connections. PJM covers 13 Mid-Atlantic and Midwest states and faces a roughly 6.8 gigawatt electricity supply shortfall. The proposal would reduce the study process length to 12 months from two years. PJM is asking the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to begin a 60-day comment period and issue a ruling within 120 days.

In real estate, a major trust acquired data centers linked to Amazon Web Services. The Blackstone real estate investment trust acquired a majority interest in two joint ventures with Amazon Web Services.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

In 1999, the Mars Climate Orbiter approached the red planet to begin its mission. NASA engineers waited in the control room for a routine orbital insertion. Deep in the flight software, a tiny human error hid in plain sight. One team used metric Newtons for thrust calculations, while another used imperial pound-seconds. The discrepancy was never caught during peer reviews. As the orbiter attempted its burn, the navigation system miscalculated the trajectory. It descended too low into the Martian atmosphere, lost structural integrity, and vaporized in the thin air, costing $125 million. It is striking how the success of a complex machine can depend entirely on basic agreement. How many small details in your own work rely on everyone speaking the exact same language?

Thank you for listening to this edition of the Sift Daily Briefing.

audioBriefIndepth.script:
Welcome to your Sift In-Depth Briefing. This is our full analysis of today's major global stories.

Why are the leaders of the United States, China, and Russia preparing for a historic joint meeting? The short answer is that presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin are set to meet in China to discuss major global conflicts like the war in Ukraine. 

For years, the world has been divided by cold wars, trade disputes, and shifting alliances. The United States and its Western allies have long opposed Russia's push to control its neighbors. Russia's president, Vladimir Putin, launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine to stop that country from joining Western defensive alliances. China's leader, Xi Jinping, has maintained close ties with Moscow while trying to keep trade open with the West. Donald Trump returned to the White House promising to end these conflicts quickly through personal diplomacy. 

The situation turned into breaking news when Ukraine struck Russia's Crimean bridge for the second night in a row, shutting it down. At the same time, Russia hit two major bridges in Kyiv with ballistic missiles. These intense attacks happened just days before the scheduled summit. 

Today, we know that Ukraine launched a massive wave of more than 1,400 drones across nineteen Russian regions. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin reported that more than 800 of those drones headed toward the capital itself. In return, Russian missiles damaged the Northern and Southern bridges in Kyiv, disrupting heating and water in parts of the city. 

This is happening right now because the three world leaders are gathering in Shenzhen, China, for a regional summit. President Trump told reporters that the war in Ukraine will be among the topics they discuss, even though the White House previously signaled it would not be on the agenda. Ukraine's leaders worry this meeting could lead to a carved-up redistribution of power, similar to the historic 1945 Yalta summit where world powers redrew borders. 

For the listener, this means the highest-level diplomacy is back, but it is happening against a backdrop of escalating war. If these talks fail, the fighting could intensify as another harsh winter sets in. You should watch to see if the leaders announce any ceasefire plans, or if the talks break down completely. 

Now let us turn to our second story, which is about advanced computer chips and global security. 

Why is the tech giant Nvidia warning its chip buyers about legal risks? The short answer is that proposed U.S. laws and new rules on cloud computing could expose both Nvidia and its customers to legal action if Chinese firms gain remote access to powerful artificial intelligence chips. 

For years, the United States has tried to keep its most advanced computer hardware out of China to protect America's lead in artificial intelligence. Tech companies like Nvidia make graphics processing units, which are the specialized computer chips needed to train powerful AI systems. Because the U.S. government restricted direct sales of these chips to China, Chinese artificial intelligence labs began looking for workarounds. They started renting overseas data centers in Europe and Asia to access Nvidia's technology remotely through the cloud. 

The situation changed when U.S. lawmakers proposed a bill called the Remote Access Security Act, or RASA. This proposed law would give the U.S. Commerce Department the tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centers to access American chips. 

Today, we learn that Nvidia messaged its chip buyers in recent months to warn them about this new legal risk. The company told clients that RASA would give the U.S. government control over cloud services in the same way it controls physical hardware. To stay ahead of the rules, Nvidia told customers it would not sell chips to anyone who rents more than 50 percent of their graphics processing units to Chinese companies. 

This is happening now because the U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security just announced an interim final rule to block Chinese remote access to AI chips. This also follows reports that Chinese labs have been actively trying to use European data centers to bypass existing trade rules. 

For the listener, this means the battle over artificial intelligence is moving from physical shipping ports into invisible cloud networks. You should watch to see if the U.S. Senate passes the RASA bill into law, and how strict the government's enforcement will be on global data centers. 

That leads us to our final story for today, which looks at public opinion and political pressure in America. 

Why is U.S. President Donald Trump's approval rating holding near a career low? The short answer is that public support has dropped because an ongoing war with Iran has pushed fuel prices sharply higher, hurting Americans' personal finances. 

For years, political parties in the United States have grown deeply divided over foreign wars and economic policies. Donald Trump won the presidency again with promises of economic strength, but his administration soon found itself entangled in a costly conflict with Iran. That war disrupted global energy markets and drove fuel prices up across the United States, creating financial pain for everyday families who need gasoline and diesel to get to work. 

The situation turned into a major political crisis when voters went to the polls in the November third midterm elections. Because voters were angry about the economy and the war, they punished the president's party at the ballot box. 

Today, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll shows that President Trump's approval rating sits at 32 percent. That rate has held steady in four straight polls since mid-October, when his rating hit a career low of 31 percent. The poll also found that just 31 percent of Americans support the war in Iran. Meanwhile, Democratic leaders in the Senate are also facing internal friction from party members who want a different approach to foreign policy. 

This is happening right now because the midterm election results mean a newly empowered Democratic majority will take control of Congress in January. Political leaders are jockeying for position and testing their public support while voters deal with the ongoing fallout from high energy costs. 

For the listener, this means public anger over the economy can quickly reshape the balance of political power in Washington. You should watch for upcoming congressional leadership votes and see if fuel prices begin to fall or stay high as winter approaches. 

Now let us look ahead to our next story, where the United States loses its measles elimination status as cases surge nationwide.

How did the United States lose its status of being free of measles? The U.S. has lost its measles elimination status because measles cases have jumped to over 5,400 this year, which is more than double last year's total. 

Decades ago, measles was a very common illness that infected millions of children every year and caused hundreds of deaths. Then in 1963, a shot called the measles vaccine became widely available, so cases dropped sharply. Because most people got the shot, the U.S. reached a point where the disease stopped spreading locally. That meant the country achieved measles elimination status in 2000, and it kept that status for over twenty-five years because vaccination rates stayed high. 

Over the last few years, childhood vaccination rates declined in many communities around the U.S. When fewer people get the shot, gaps open up in population immunity, so a small outbreak no longer fizzles out. Instead, ongoing chains of transmission can take root. 

Because of those gaps, the U.S. recorded 2,242 measles cases in 2025. That was the most cases in over three decades. 

That record was broken this year when the U.S. tallied 5,412 cases to date in 2026. The Pan American Health Organization confirmed the loss of elimination status on Saturday. The Pan American Health Organization is a regional office for the World Health Organization covering North and South America. The CDC reports that this year's cases have resulted in more than 590 hospitalizations and at least six measles-related deaths. The biggest outbreak is in Pennsylvania, with more than 1,500 cases and seven deaths. Almost all of the cases have been in people who were not vaccinated. 

This is happening now because population immunity lowered enough that the U.S. failed the World Health Organization standard of having no locally transmitted outbreaks lasting twelve months or longer. 

This means you could be at risk of exposure if you are not vaccinated, and hospitals need to watch for measles in anyone with a fever and rash. Senator Bill Cassidy, a Republican doctor from Louisiana, warned that unvaccinated people could bring death to vulnerable children who are too young to get the shot. Experts say the country needs to return to higher rates of vaccination, ramp up vaccination campaigns, and battle misinformation to curb outbreaks. For next steps, watch your state lawmakers, because nine states made opting out easier in 2025, and state legislatures will write exemption rules when they reconvene in January. 

Meanwhile, why is the U.S. dollar rising while other markets shift? The U.S. dollar held at April 2025 highs on Monday as markets awaited comments from U.S. Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh. 

The U.S. Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States that sets interest rates to manage the economy. Over recent years, the Fed raised interest rates to fight inflation, which is the rising cost of goods. Higher interest rates make a currency more attractive to global investors who want a better return on their money. 

The dollar index advanced for a fifth straight day, up 0.1 percent at 103.52, which is its highest level in 19 months. The greenback was buoyed last week after hawkish comments from several Fed officials and hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data raised bets for a quicker pace of rate hikes. Hawkish means officials favor higher interest rates to keep inflation down. Traders using the CME Group FedWatch tool have priced in an implied 89.7 percent probability of a 25-basis-point hike at the next Fed meeting on December 9. 

This is happening now because investors are looking for clues on the U.S. interest rate outlook ahead of Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh's appearance. 

This means the dollar is strong right now, but it could face pressure if dovish Fed policymakers push back or if upcoming tech earnings disappoint. Bitcoin also fell 1.2 percent to 64,261 dollars, remaining fragile after a weekend rout. Watch for the Fed meeting on December 9 and upcoming tech reports to see if the dollar's rally continues. 

Also, why is the European Union accusing Russia of stalling peace talks? The European Union says Russia is trying to drag out talks on ending the war in Ukraine while it bombs power plants to make life harder as winter closes in. 

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, starting a war that is now nearing its fifth year. In that time, Russia has bombed civilian infrastructure to weaken Ukraine. For just over a year, U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have talked to Russia and Ukraine as mediators, but no lasting ceasefire has been agreed. 

Last week, after negotiations in Abu Dhabi, the United States encouraged Ukraine and its backers to agree to a Russian demand for a new security framework for Europe. The Europeans likened this to the treaty Russia offered NATO before the 2022 war, because it asks the military alliance to pull troops and equipment back westward. European leaders see this as a Russian attempt to weaken NATO. 

At talks in Brussels on Monday, European Union foreign ministers rejected the new demands. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russia is using the demands as a pretext for keeping the war going while continuing attacks. 

This is happening now because winter is closing in, and the European Union wants to secure a ceasefire rather than accept fresh demands from Russia. 

The EU also imposed sanctions on nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions on Monday, along with asset freezes and travel bans on others accused of spreading propaganda. Europe's role will focus on security arrangements, reconstruction, and Ukraine's future, while only Ukraine can decide on its sovereignty. Watch for future talks involving Europe's team of security advisers to see if a ceasefire can be reached. 

That leads directly into our next story, which is about how the energy transition only works if development works.

How can an energy transition succeed if it causes economic pain? The shift works only when it improves people's lives and supports macroeconomic stability, which means keeping prices steady and economies growing.

Across Asia and the Pacific, countries are trying to move away from fossil fuel energy, which is coal and oil that release greenhouse gases. This shift can cause inflation and political backlash if it is not managed well. Energy is a core economic variable. Its domestic price influences inflation, and its import costs affect trade balances. Subsidies for fossil fuels also take up money that could go to infrastructure and health.

Indonesia showed what is possible in two thousand fourteen when oil prices declined. The government decreased gasoline subsidies. This reduced explicit energy subsidy spending from three point two percent to one point zero percent of gross domestic product in a single year, and redirected the savings into infrastructure and social protection.

Now, the Economic and Social Survey of Asia and the Pacific two thousand six argues that transition policy must become development policy. The report proposes a structured framework for identifying priority national energy transition goals, such as expanding clean energy or improving energy efficiency. India's solar manufacturing incentive scheme catalyzed forty-eight gigawatts of manufacturing capacity and is projected to save about one point eight billion dollars annually in foreign exchange. Nepal expanded electricity coverage from fifty-three percent to ninety-five percent of the total population between two thousand ten and two thousand twenty-four. This moved the national utility from chronic deficit to profitability, while reliable power saved the economy an estimated six to seven percent of gross domestic product annually.

This is happening now because countries face overlapping structural challenges from energy systems that are tied to volatile fossil fuels and pressing climate targets.

For the listener, this means that energy rules will succeed only if they bring visible economic gains. Watch for whether upcoming policies in the region can balance decarbonization with job creation and cost control.

What can a map of tiny brain structures reveal about treating major diseases? Researchers have built a detailed cellular atlas of the basal ganglia, which are clusters of cells tucked beneath the cortex that are key to learning and controlling motor skills.

The human brain is incredibly complex and contains more than eighty billion neurons. Within it, the basal ganglia occupy about two percent of the brain volume, which is about the size of a gumball. Michael Hawrylycz, a senior investigator at the Allen Institute, and his colleague Hongkui Zeng explain that these structures are key to controlling movements, making decisions, and forming habits. Because of that, the basal ganglia are also implicated in several major brain diseases, including neurodegenerative diseases like Parkinson's and Huntington's, as well as schizophrenia, depression, bipolar disorder, and addiction.

Scientists wanted to map this structure because it is shared across many species, allowing researchers to understand the differences between humans and other primates. A consortium of researchers looked at more than twenty-five million cells from the brains of humans, macaques, and marmosets.

Now, they have published an atlas of this part of the brain as a package of papers in Cell Press. This is the culmination of three years of intense scientific work funded mainly by the National Institutes of Health, involving researchers at more than fifty institutions around the world. Satrajit Ghosh, a senior scientist at the McGovern Institute for Brain Research at MIT, compares this effort to the Human Genome Project from the nineties, which gave scientists a common foundation for their research. Talia Lerner, a researcher at the Center for Addiction and Mental Health in Toronto, notes that current Parkinson's medications can have severe side effects like pathological gambling, which precise maps might help eliminate by enabling targeted medicines.

This research is happening now because teams have finished three years of intense work and released their findings to the scientific community.

For the listener, this means scientists are building a template for the entire brain. Watch for whether researchers meet their expectation to have a dataset for the whole brain by the end of next year.

How is a small country powering homes and transport using pig waste? Denmark is converting livestock manure into biogas, which supplies the national grid.

Pigs are big business in Denmark, accounting for a quarter of the country's food exports. There are as many as twelve million breeding pigs in the country at any one time, which is more than double the human population. That ratio spirals when accounting for thirty million more pigs produced for slaughter and live export every year. Managing this animal waste has long been a challenge. According to the Danish Agriculture and Food Council, Denmark's pig sector annually produces more than seventeen million tonnes of manure, mostly liquid slurry, which emits considerable greenhouse gases like methane and nitrous oxide.

Over the last decade, Denmark has upscaled a handful of small biogas operations into about one hundred fifty industrial-sized plants. Up to seventy percent of the processed raw materials come from pig and cattle manure. Today, Denmark has Europe's highest share of biogas in its gas grid, at about forty percent.

Now, this biogas boom is benefiting towns like Sonderborg. An initiative called ProjectZero, established in two thousand seven, aimed to create a carbon-neutral energy system by the end of twenty twenty-nine. The combined use of renewables, industrial waste heat, and biogas has cut energy-related carbon emissions by seventy-nine percent. Two large-scale biogas facilities in Sonderborg use approximately eight hundred fifty thousand tonnes of organic material annually, producing enough biogas to cover all of the Sonderborg region's annual gas demand. However, a report by NOAH Friends of the Earth Denmark and Foodrise argues that this reliance creates a factory farm trap that maintains high livestock numbers.

This is happening now because volatile oil and gas markets, caused by conflicts in Ukraine and Iran, make local energy solutions more urgent.

For the listener, this means agricultural waste can become a primary fuel source. Watch for how Denmark implements its upcoming carbon tax on agriculture in twenty thirty, where farmers will pay about sixteen euros, or eighteen dollars, for every tonne of carbon dioxide they emit.

That brings us to our next story, which explores how Shanghai has climbed to the number two maritime hub as China pushes to grow its shipping clout.

Shanghai has reached its highest-ever global ranking for port operations. The Chinese megacity rose to second place in a ranking of major global maritime hubs. It reached this position as China expands its footprint in global shipping amid a complex trade environment, securing the spot largely on the strength of its combined industrial and tech power.

How can the biggest power grid in America fix long wait times for data center power? 

PJM Interconnection is proposing a plan to federal regulators to speed up power connections, but data center companies may have to pay more for grid costs. 

PJM Interconnection is the biggest electric grid operator in the United States. It covers thirteen Mid-Atlantic and Midwest states, a region with sixty-seven million Americans. For years, electricity grids were built to power homes and standard businesses, not giant computer warehouses. 

Big Tech companies began a rapid data center expansion roughly three years ago. These data centers are giant buildings filled with servers that need massive amounts of electricity to run artificial intelligence and cloud computing. 

Because data centers use so much power, the demand grew much faster than the supply. That supply and demand crunch triggered a sharp rise in power bills for people living in the region. It also created a six point eight gigawatt electricity supply shortfall. A gigawatt is a huge amount of power, enough to light millions of homes. This shortfall threatens the reliability of the grid if new power supplies are not secured on time. 

PJM has struggled to keep up with these rising electricity needs. The grid operator has a long study process that is required before hooking up a power plant or a large data center. PJM wants to combine its separate processes of studying power generation, transmission lines, and large loads like data centers. 

PJM announced on Monday that it is proposing this new plan to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. 

Under the new plan, the length of the study process would be reduced to twelve months from two years. PJM spokesman Jeff Shields said neither generation nor transmission is coming online quickly enough to keep pace with new demand growth. He added that the factor PJM planning can influence is how quickly these new resources are studied for reliability. 

By combining the planning process, PJM will be able to identify exactly where the grid needs upgrades. That will give states and utilities clear information about transmission costs driven by data centers. Then utilities can bill the data center companies directly, instead of spreading the costs across other users. 

This change is happening now because the current delays threaten the reliability of the grid, and power bills are rising for millions of people. 

Data center advocates pushed back against earlier discussions of this combined process. The trade group Data Centre Coalition told the PJM board in October that the combined process might complicate the grid interconnection process and lead to longer delays. 

PJM is asking the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to begin a sixty-day comment period on the plan and issue a ruling within one hundred twenty days. For the listener, this means data center companies could face higher costs and faster connection times, while the rest of us watch to see if the grid stays stable. 

Blackstone Reit acquired data centers linked to Amazon Web Services. The trust acquired a majority interest in two joint ventures with Amazon Web Services. 

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

In 1999, the Mars Climate Orbiter approached the red planet to begin its mission. NASA engineers waited in the control room, expecting a routine orbital insertion as the craft dipped behind the horizon. 

Deep in the flight software, a tiny human error hid in plain sight. One team used metric Newtons for thrust calculations. Another team used imperial pound-seconds. The discrepancy was never caught during peer reviews. 

As the orbiter attempted its burn, the navigation system miscalculated the trajectory. It descended too low into the Martian atmosphere. It lost structural integrity under the friction, and it vaporized in the thin, alien air. 

The universe does not forgive a rounding error. A project costing one hundred twenty-five million dollars was lost because two teams used different measuring systems. 

It reminds us that tiny details matter deeply when we build complex systems. 

What system in your own life relies on a measurement you have never checked? 

I am so glad you joined me for this part of Sift In-Depth. Take good care of yourself, and I will see you next time.

Will the leaders of the United States, China, and Russia meet for a historic summit? Yes, President Donald Trump is traveling to China to meet with China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's President Vladimir Putin.

For years, relations between these three powerful nations have been very tense. The United States and Russia have been deeply opposed over Russia's war in Ukraine, which has dragged on for almost five years. At the same time, the United States and China have clashed over trade rules and advanced computer chips. Because each country wants more global influence, they often find themselves at odds on the world stage.

Then things heated up right before the meeting. Ukraine launched drone strikes on Russia's Crimean bridge for the second night in a row. This shut down the bridge, which carries both cars and trains. At the same time, Russia fired ballistic missiles at two major bridges in Kyiv, which is the capital of Ukraine. Russia's defence ministry said it downed one thousand four hundred forty-one Ukrainian drones in a major overnight barrage. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned of this attack ahead of the upcoming talks.

Now, President Trump has arrived in Asia for a multiday trip. He is visiting the Philippines first for regional meetings, and then he will travel to Shenzhen, China. On Thursday, he is scheduled to hold a joint meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. The White House said the talks are expected to center on decreasing the spread of nuclear weapons. President Trump told reporters they would also discuss the war in Ukraine and the conflict with Iran. Tesla and SpaceX chief executive officer Elon Musk is expected to join the trip, but he will not be in the room for the meeting with Putin and Xi.

This is happening right now because diplomatic efforts to end the war in Ukraine have stalled as winter approaches. Russia wants a sweeping deal to rewrite Europe's security architecture, including curbs on NATO. NATO is a military alliance of European and North American countries. Meanwhile, Ukraine and its allies want a ceasefire first, and President Zelenskyy has warned that the summit could lead to a Yalta-like redistribution of global power. The original Yalta summit happened in nineteen forty-five, when allied leaders carved up post-World War II territories.

For the listener, this summit could shape the future of global conflicts and nuclear weapons agreements. But the talks may not bring an immediate peace deal, because the countries want very different things. Could tech companies face legal trouble if Chinese firms remotely rent their artificial intelligence chips? Yes, Nvidia has warned chip buyers that proposed legislation could expose both the chipmaker and its customers to U.S. legal action.

Nvidia is a massive American chip designer that makes powerful processors for artificial intelligence. U.S. export controls restrict these advanced chips from going directly to China. Because of these rules, Chinese tech companies have been looking for ways to use the chips from afar. They try to rent data centers overseas so they can access the computing power without buying the physical hardware.

Then the United States government stepped up its efforts to close this loophole. Lawmakers proposed a new bill called the Remote Access Security Act, or RASA. This bill would give the U.S. Commerce Department the tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centers. In response to this pressure, Nvidia started messaging its chip buyers in recent months to explain the new risks.

Now, Nvidia is telling its customers that the proposed legislation could expose everyone involved to legal trouble. Because of this, the chipmaker says it will not sell chips to customers who rent more than fifty percent of their graphics processing units to Chinese companies. These are specialized processors that power artificial intelligence systems. Separately, the U.S. Commerce Department announced an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies from remotely accessing these AI chips.

This is happening now because U.S. officials want to maintain the country's lead in the artificial intelligence race. Chinese labs, such as Moonshot AI, have recently sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe and East Asia. At the same time, Nvidia is facing a leadership shakeup after its former chief executive officer, Jensen Huang, stepped down amid reports of a personal relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China. Why did the United States just lose its special status for beating the measles? The country lost its measles elimination status because reported cases surged past five thousand four hundred this year, which is more than double last year's total. 

To understand how we got here, we have to look back at how the United States used to fight this disease. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention started collecting national data on measles way back in nineteen twelve. In the first decade of those records, about six thousand people died from measles every year. By the nineteen fifties, nearly every child in the United States caught measles before turning fifteen.
